title: Oriented ion migration in dielectric Sb_4O_5Cl_2 single crystals for multifunctional two-dimensional electronics

paper_content.abstract: Exploring dielectrics with high gate capacitance and artificial tailoring of electronic states is highly desirable for the development of 2D electronics. Here, we report the synthesis of a single-crystalline ionic dielectric Sb4O5Cl2 with aligned ionic channels, achieving a dielectric constant of 23.3 (at a thickness of ~25 nm) and non-volatile programmable regulation of the ionic migration. The fabricated 2D MoS2 transistors display on/off ratios up to 109, leakage currents down to 10−14 A, and mobility of 33.4 cm2 V−1 s−1. Oriented ionic channels facilitate efficient and controllable migration of Cl− ions, thus realizing a non-structural-damage and reconfigurable transition between a quasi-metallic and semiconducting state in MoS2, with a retention time exceeding 3000 s. During 100 cycles of state transitions, the quasi-metallic state exhibits a conductivity of 10−5 S, which is 103 times that of the semiconducting state. Bio-inspired ionic channel further allows neuromorphic devices to integrate image storage, processing, and recognition capabilities, achieving a recognition accuracy improvement from 80.7% to 90.9% within just 5 training epochs through non-volatile preprocessing lasting over 300 s. Our study highlights the significant potential of this single-crystal ionic dielectric as a promising platform for fundamental research on electronic state modulation and advanced electronics.
paper_content.introduction:
Two-dimensional (2D) electronics have emerged as an ideal platform for studying exotic quantum physics, new functional transistors, and novel computing paradigms, owing to the quantum size effects, the tunable electronic structures, and the strong coupling interactions with external fields of 2D materials1–8. To meet the demands of increasingly complex functionalities, gate dielectrics need not only high dielectric constants to address device-scaling challenges9–12, but also artificial tailoring of electronic states13,14. This dual functionality may allow monolithic integration of multiple operational modes within a single device architecture, such as combining high-performance field-effect transistors (FETs) for digital logic operations15–17, reversible phase transition for analog memory programming18,19, and neuromorphic computing20,21 or other advanced functions. Yet now, conventional metal oxide dielectrics (such as Al2O3, SiO2, and HfO2) still face challenges including low dielectric constants, amorphous structures, and incompatible interfaces induced by dangling bonds, which hinders further miniaturization of devices, limited carrier modulation capabilities and lacking memory characteristics22–26.

In recent years, ionic gate dielectrics have attracted significant attention due to their high-κ dielectric constants from ionic polarization27–29 and the extremely high electric fields enabled by the electric double layer (EDL) of ions30–33, which can significantly enhance the capability of modulating electronic states in 2D materials inducing discrete superconducting phases34, strong Ising-type spin-orbit coupling33, and quenching the bandgap of 2D semiconductors32. However, conventional ionic dielectrics (liquid or solid electrolytes, primarily amorphous or polycrystalline structures) still present formidable challenges including poor compatibility with 2D materials, disordered ion migration pathways leading to random electrical performance and irreversible lattice damage caused by ion-migration resulting in poor stability, thereby severely limiting further research35–38.

In this work, we report a single-crystalline ionic dielectric Sb4O5Cl2, possessing a high κ exceeding 23.3 (~25 nm) and oriented ion-migration paths to address the above mentioned long-term issues. Benefiting from the high κ value and van der Waals structure, 2D transistors exhibit high on/off ratio (109) at a low operation voltage (Vds = 0.5 V), low leakage current (10−14 A), and high room-temperature mobility of 33.4 cm2 V−1 s−1, and realize NOT (inverter), AND, and NAND logic functions. The periodic ionic channels within the single-crystalline structure enhance the efficiency of ionic migration while achieving precise control and non-volatile characteristics. By electrically modulating the ionic states in Sb4O5Cl2, a reversible transition between quasi-metallic and semiconducting states in MoS2 channels has been achieved. This reconfigurability remains stable over 100 cycles and exhibits good retention under both room-temperature and elevated-temperature conditions (over 40 min). The quasi-metallic state shows a conductivity of ~10−5 S, surpassing the semiconducting state by three orders of magnitude, while the ion on/off ratios differ by six orders. Based on this, the device shows good memory properties with good retention (more than 3000 s) and endurance (over 1000 cycles). Furthermore, synapse-like functions integrating image storage, processing, and recognition have been realized. Owing to the non-volatile preprocessing capability lasting over 300 s, the recognition accuracy reaches 90.9% after just 5 training epochs. In summary, our research not only provides a material platform for high-performance 2D electronic devices but also demonstrates its potential in fields such as fundamental studies and multifunctional devices.
paper_content.results:
Characterization of Sb4O5Cl2 and theory calculations
The Sb4O5Cl2 single crystal, a type of ionic layered material crystallizing in the monoclinic system with space group P2/c (No. 14, a=6.16 Å, b=5.14 Å, c=13.62 Å), features an alternating stack of negatively charged [Cl]2n- anion layers and positively charged [Sb4O5]2n+ layers along the a-axis, exhibiting an interlayer spacing of approximately 6.16 Å (the left part of Fig. 1a). Notably, the Sb and O atoms in the [Sb4O5]2n+ layers are not densely packed. Instead, they form [SbO] eight-membered rings, which align precisely with the interlayer Cl− ions, thereby creating a pathway for Cl− ions migration along the a-axis between layers (the right part of Fig. 1a). Compared with amorphous and polycrystalline ionic materials, the oriented ion-migration within such a single-crystal system under external stimulus facilitates higher ionic concentration accumulation at interfaces, thereby inducing enhanced modulation and coupling effects. The synthesis method of Sb4O5Cl2 single crystals is provided in Methods and Supplementary Fig. 1. The as-synthesized centimeter-scale Sb4O5Cl2 single crystals exhibit three intense and sharp diffraction peaks assigned to the {100} crystallographic planes (Fig. 1b). Although the interlayers in Sb4O5Cl2 are bonded via weak electrostatic interactions-making it more difficult to exfoliate than traditional van der Waals 2D materials-nanosheets were still obtained using a thermally assisted tape exfoliation and transfer method (see Supplementary Fig. 2 and Methods). The obtained Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheets were further confirmed by Raman spectroscopy, and the vibrational modes of their characteristic peaks are assigned via angle-resolved polarized Raman measurements (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4). These characterizations indicate the highly crystalline layered structure of the as-synthesized Sb4O5Cl2 crystals.

To further elucidate the structure of Sb4O5Cl2, high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) characterization was conducted on Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheets. As shown in Fig. 1c, d and Supplementary Fig. 5, we performed HAADF-STEM imaging along different crystallographic orientations of Sb4O5Cl2, namely, [010], [100], and [001], all of which match well with the structure model and lattice spacing of Sb4O5Cl2. Given the contrast dependence of HAADF-STEM on the atomic number (Z) and atomic occupancy39–41, atomic columns containing different quantities of Sb (Z=51) are clearly identified. Notably, the unique interlayer Cl− ions sandwiched between [Sb4O5]2n+ layers can be distinctly observed (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 6) with an interlayer spacing of 6.16 Å. The measured lattice spacings of 6.81 Å and 5.14 Å correspond to the (002) and (010) lattice planes, respectively. While O atoms remain indiscernible due to their weak contrast arising from a low atomic number, Cl− ions confined within the [SbO] rings are clearly resolved with discernible intensity (Supplementary Fig. 7). Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping shows a uniform elemental distribution with an atomic ratio of Sb/O/Cl close to 4:5:2 (Supplementary Fig. 8). Furthermore, high-resolution EDS analysis along the [010] zone axis reveals an alternating stacked distribution of Sb and Cl elements (Fig. 1e), in agreement with the corresponding TEM image. Figure 1f displays the contrast intensity profile extracted along the orange dashed line crossing the [Sb4O5]2n+ layers and the pink dashed line situated within the interlayer regions from Fig. 1c. The profile distinctly reveals the periodic arrangement of Sb and Cl, along with the occupancy of Cl within the interlayer positions. The chemical states of Sb4O5Cl2 were further characterized by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), where the Cl 2p spectral feature centered at a binding energy of 197.7 eV provides conclusive evidence for the existence of interlayer Cl− ions (Supplementary Fig. 9).

We calculated the band structures of Sb4O5Cl2 using density functional theory (Fig. 1g). Sb4O5Cl2 exhibits a large indirect bandgap of ~3.7 eV, whose conduction band minimum (CBM) and valence band maximum (VBM) are located at Z and Γ point of the first Brillouin zone, respectively. Furthermore, the band structure of Sb4O5Cl2 was experimentally determined by ultraviolet-visible absorption spectrum and ultraviolet photoelectron spectrum (UPS) with a bandgap of ~3.9 eV (Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. 10), in good agreement with the calculated band structures. Such a wide bandgap renders Sb4O5Cl2 an insulator, as ascertained by the conductive test of a two-terminal device and its resistivity of over 1010 Ω·cm at 300 K can be extracted from the Ids-Vds curve (Supplementary Fig. 11).

Dielectric properties of Sb4O5Cl2
The theoretical dielectric constant of Sb4O5Cl2 was also calculated in Fig. 2a. Sb4O5Cl2 exhibits high dielectric constants across all three crystallographic directions, predominantly originating from ionic polarization (with electronic polarization contributing merely ~5 to the total permittivity). This observation highlights the strong ionic character of Sb4O5Cl2, which arises from its unique crystal structure. Notably, the highest dielectric constant of 32.9 is observed along the a-axis (perpendicular to the [Sb4O5]2n+ layers), which is consistent with the direction of the Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheets obtained by mechanical exfoliation, suggesting a high dielectric controllability of electronic states. The parallel-plate capacitors with vertical metal-insulator-metal (MIM) structure were further fabricated16, as shown in the inset of Fig. 2b. The effective dielectric constant (εeff) of Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheets can be calculated by the equation C = Aε0εeff/t, where C is the measured capacitance, A is the overlapping area of top and bottom electrodes, ε0 is the vacuum dielectric constant and t is the physical thickness of Sb4O5Cl2. The εeff of the 190 nm Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheet, derived from capacitance-frequency (C-f) measurement (Fig. 2b), reaches around 29.5 at 100 kHz and this experimental value aligns remarkably well with theoretical calculations. Thickness-dependent εeff is shown in Fig. 2c. Despite thickness-dependent reduction, Sb4O5Cl2 achieves a dielectric constant of up to 43.2 and maintains a value above 17.5 even at ~15 nm, attributable to its strong ionic polarization mechanism. Additionally, the leakage current and corresponding breakdown field strength of Sb4O5Cl2 were demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 12, revealing a breakdown field of 3 MV cm−1 while maintaining leakage current below the dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) limit9. The relationship between the bandgap and corresponding dielectric constant of currently reported dielectrics was plotted in Fig. 2d9–11,17,28,29,39,42–47, demonstrating that Sb4O5Cl2 single crystal possesses a relatively higher dielectric constant (as evidenced by εeff = 3.3 for h-BN, εeff = 16.5 for β-Bi2SeO5, εeff = 11.5 for Sb2O3, εeff = 8.4 for CaF2 and εeff = 15.3 for GdOCl).

Single-crystalline ionic dielectric Sb4O5Cl2 for 2D transistors
To examine the potential of Sb4O5Cl2 as a dielectric in devices, MoS2 FETs with Sb4O5Cl2 as the bottom-gate dielectric were fabricated on the SiO2/Si substrate, utilizing exfoliated few-layer graphene (FLG) as gate electrode and In/Au as the source and drain electrodes. Figure 2e shows linear Ids-Vds curves under different gate voltages (Vg), indicating well electrical contacts. The transfer characteristics are presented in Fig. 2f, presenting a high on/off ratio (Ion/Ioff) exceeding 109 at a low operation voltage (Vds = 0.5 V). It is worth noting that even when the operation voltage of Vds is as low as 0.05 V, the transistor still maintains a high Ion/Ioff of 108. Moreover, the device exhibits a low leakage current (~10−14 A) throughout the entire testing process. Furthermore, field-effect mobility of the device reaches 33.4 cm2 V−1 s−1 by linear fitting the transfer curve (Vds = 1 V). The high Ion/Ioff and charge carrier mobility are fundamentally attributed to the superior dielectric constant of Sb4O5Cl2, which originates from robust ionic polarization effects enabled by its ordered ionic migration channels. And the performance of 20 FETs devices was tested and statistically analyzed, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 13. The results demonstrate that the devices exhibit relatively excellent performance in terms of Ion/Ioff, threshold voltage, and mobility, with relatively small variations observed between different devices. Additionally, we fabricated and characterized a top-gated MoS2 device with a Sb4O5Cl2 single-crystal dielectric layer thinner than 100 nm (Supplementary Fig. 14), which also exhibits a high Ion/Ioff exceeding 108. Compared with the 2D transistors with state-of-the-art high-κ dielectrics, our devices exhibit stronger gate controllability (as shown in Fig. 2g), exhibiting higher Ion/Ioff under low operation voltage and much lower leakage current9–11,17,28,29,39,43,44. To evaluate the stability of the Sb4O5Cl2 ionic single-crystal dielectric layer, we conducted positive bias temperature instability (PBTI) and time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) tests on the MoS2/Sb4O5Cl2/FLG device, and the results are presented in Supplementary Fig. 15.

We also fabricated logic circuits based on MoS2/Sb4O5Cl2 and MoTe2/Sb4O5Cl2 FETs. Supplementary Fig. 16 illustrates the most essential NOT gate (also known as an inverter), which exhibits sharp switching characteristics at different VDD values. More complicated logic units such as the AND gate and the NAND gate were also fabricated (Supplementary Fig. 17). The AND gate and NAND gate operate at VDD of 2.0 V to perform their logical functions. Our results confirm the application potential of the Sb4O5Cl2 ionic single-crystal dielectric layer in logic circuits.

Reconfigurable transition of MoS2
The ion-electron coupling between Sb4O5Cl2 and MoS2 can effectively modulate the carrier concentration in MoS2, thereby further inducing changes in the electrical properties of MoS2. As illustrated in Fig. 3a, the top Sb4O5Cl2 layer functions as a modulation layer, not merely a dielectric. It regulates the direction of Cl− ion migration within itself by adjusting the top ionic gate voltage (Vionic), thus controlling the carrier concentration in MoS2. The SiO2/Si back-gate, in contrast, is used to characterize the modulated electrical behavior of the MoS2 channel.

The Ids-Vds and back-gate transfer characteristics under varying Vionic (+10 V and −10 V for 20 s) are characterized, with the results presented in Fig. 3b, c, respectively. From the Ids-Vds curves, it can be observed that, compared to pristine MoS2, a positive Vionic suppresses Ids while a negative Vionic enhances Ids, which indicates that applying Vionic can effectively modulate the conductivity of MoS2. From the back-gate transfer characteristics, a positive Vionic enhances the n-type semiconductor behavior of MoS2, increasing the Ion/Ioff from 106 to 107. In contrast, after applying a negative Vionic, the device maintains a high conductance state (Ids ~ 10−5 A) throughout the back-gate sweep process, and the Ion/Ioff is less than 10, indicating the transition from semiconducting to quasi-metallic characteristics. Importantly, unlike structure-destructive and irreversible atomic doping48,49, the transition of MoS2 between quasi-metallic and semiconducting state enabled by the modulated Cl− ions of Sb4O5Cl2 exhibits non-destructive nature and high reversibility. By applying gradually increasing negative and positive Vionic to the Sb4O5Cl2 modulation layer, a stepwise transition of MoS2 between semiconducting and quasi-metallic state was achieved, as shown in Fig. 3d, e, respectively. We also tested the retention characteristics of both states at room temperature and elevated temperatures (Supplementary Fig. 18). The state could be maintained for over 40 min even at 100 °C. Furthermore, (Ids-T) curves after different pulsed Vionic demonstrate that the conductance retention can exceed 3000 s (Supplementary Fig. 19). These results indicate that the reconfigurable modulation exhibits a certain degree of non-volatility, and based on this, we successfully fabricated a memory device with good retention (>3000 s) and endurance (>1000 cycles), as shown in Supplementary Fig. 20.

Notably, this reconfigurable transition exhibits good cycling stability. As shown in Fig. 3f, the device underwent 100 cycles of positive-negative Vionic switching while maintaining stable state transfer characteristics. With increasing cycling times, both the quasi-metallic and semiconducting state exhibit minimal fluctuations in Ion/Ioff (Fig. 3g). After 100 cycles, the quasi-metallic state retains an Ion/Ioff below 10, while the semiconducting state maintains a high Ion/Ioff of 105. As demonstrated in Fig. 3h, the quasi-metallic state consistently maintains high conductance (>10−5 S), which is 103 times higher than that of the semiconducting state, while a seven-order-of-magnitude conductance contrast between the two states persists even after 100 cycling tests (Vbg = −10 V). Furthermore, the reconfiguration endurance was extended to 2000 cycles with stable performance. The performance of Sb4O5Cl2-based top-gate FETs was compared before and after cycling, and negligible degradation was observed (Supplementary Fig. 21). These results demonstrate that Sb4O5Cl2 exhibits a remarkably strong non-volatile modulation capability on the electronic states of MoS2, and owing to its unique crystal structure, the physical structural damage caused by this modulation is negligible50.

Mechanism of oriented ion-migration in Sb4O5Cl2
To elucidate the mechanism of tailoring the electronic states, theoretical calculations and systematic experiments were conducted. Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) measurements on Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheets ruled out ferroelectric behavior, supported by negligible phase hysteresis and butterfly amplitude loops40, consistent with its centrosymmetric structure (Supplementary Fig. 22). Therefore, we proposed that the migration of Cl− ions at the Sb4O5Cl2/MoS2 interface under the top ionic gate leads to the tailoring of electronic states in MoS2, enabling reconfigurable transitions between quasi-metallic and semiconducting state, as illustrated in Fig. 4a. Under negative Vionic, Cl− ions migrate and accumulate at the Sb4O5Cl2/MoS2 interface, which captures holes in the MoS2 channel, thereby generating more electrons and driving the transition of MoS2 from the initial n-type semiconductor to a quasi-metal. While under positive Vionic, Cl− ions at the interface are depleted, leading to the accumulation of Cl− vacancies (VCl). These VCl capture electrons in the MoS2 channel, reducing the electron concentration and restoring semiconducting behavior. Subsequently, we conducted band structure calculations for MoS2 at two distinct Sb4O5Cl2 interfaces-the Cl− ions interface and the VCl interface-as well as for isolated MoS2, as shown in Fig. 4b, c and Supplementary Fig. 23, respectively. The Fermi level (Ef) of isolated MoS2 is located at the VBM. However, MoS2 shows an upward Ef shift into the conduction band with Cl− ion interface, indicating n-type degenerate doping48. In contrast, the Ef of MoS2 returns to the VBM position with Cl− vacancy interfaces closely matching that of the isolated MoS2, indicating that MoS2 exhibits semiconducting properties at this state. The theoretical calculation results are in excellent agreement with the experimental data and the proposed mechanism.

Furthermore, the ion-migration paths have been calculated, as shown in Fig. 4d. The total energy of the system at each step as the Cl− ions moved through the [Sb4O5]2n+ layer was obtained by relaxing the atomic positions until the maximum force on each atom was less than 10⁻2 eV/Å. To enable efficient Cl− ions migration, the Sb-O bonds surrounding the [SbO] octagonal ring undergo sequential dissociation, driving structural reconfiguration from an octagonal ring through decagonal to dodecagonal configurations, with the entire process exhibiting an energy barrier of 2.10 eV. Compared to ion-migration barriers in other 2D material systems (Fig. 4e)51–53, the Cl− ions migration barrier in Sb4O5Cl2 single crystals is relatively lower (e.g., K+/MoS2: 2.46 eV and Ag+/graphene: 4.27 eV) indicating the inherent migration. Meanwhile, the periodic lattice potential of the single-crystalline Sb4O5Cl2 constrains Cl− migration, imparting a certain degree of non-volatility.

To further confirm this modulation mechanism, we fabricated a MoS2/Sb4O5Cl2/FLG device and employed Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) to characterize the surface potential evolution (Supplementary Fig. 24). As shown in Fig. 4f and Supplementary Fig. 25, the change in the work function is expressed by the contact potential difference (CPD) between the sample surface and the probe tip, as defined by the formula VCPD = (φtip − φsample)/q, where q is the elementary charge, φsample and φtip are the work functions of the sample surface and probe tip54,55. Compared with the pristine KPFM mapping, at Vionic = −20 V, the potential of Sb4O5Cl2 in the edge regions of MoS2 exhibits a significant decrease, which correlates with an increase in the φsample and a downwards shift of the Ef, attributed to the reduction in electron concentration resulting from the accumulation of Cl− ions. Conversely, at Vionic = +20 V, the potential of Sb4O5Cl2 at the MoS2 edges exhibits a significant increase, accompanied by an upward shift of the Ef, as Cl− ions migrate away from the interface, resulting in hole depletion and electron accumulation. Notably, the potential variation in Sb4O5Cl2 was exclusively observed within the overlap regions between the bottom FLG and the top MoS2 layer. This phenomenon is attributed to the migration of Cl− ions occurring only in areas subjected to a vertical electric field, whereas ions migration remains negligible in non-gated regions (as demarcated by the black dashed lines in Fig. 4f). The potential-distance profiles extracted along the yellow and red arrows (Fig. 4f) are shown in Fig. 4g and Supplementary Fig. 26. Initially, the regulated (left part of the black dashed line) and non-regulated (right part of the black dashed line) MoS2 regions exhibited a minor potential difference (−18.2 mV). At Vionic = −20 V, the regulated MoS2 region showed an Ef upshift and potential increase, resulting in a 110.6 mV difference compared to the non-regulated region. Conversely, at Vionic = +20 V, the potential difference reversed to −84.3 mV, indicating an Ef downshift in the regulated MoS2 region that exceeded its initial state (Fig. 4g). The Sb4O5Cl2 at MoS2 edges displayed significant potential inversion (>2 V, Supplementary Fig. 26) under alternating Vionic, driven by Cl− ions depletion and accumulation. KPFM results reveal the band structure evolution of the Sb4O5Cl2/MoS2 heterojunction under varying Vionic (Supplementary Fig. 27), with the Ef shift in MoS2 in excellent agreement with electrical and theoretical data. This highlight that the reconfigurable transition between quasi-metallic and semiconducting state in MoS2 is achieved through efficient Cl− ions migration enabled by the unique crystal structure of Sb4O5Cl2.

Neuromorphic image preprocessing and classification
Leveraging the distinct periodic crystal potential field and the tunable Cl− ions migration behavior of Sb4O5Cl2, we emulate ion-mediated conductance modulation analogous to synaptic plasticity. The detailed biological analogy and transport mechanism are provided in Supplementary Information (Supplementary Fig. 28)56,57. Under positive or negative pulse voltages (Vp), Cl− ions drift directionally within the dielectric, accumulating near or depleting from the MoS2 interface through [SbO] ring channels, as illustrated in Fig. 5a(i), b(i). This dynamic redistribution modulates the local Cl− concentration, thereby tuning the device conductance (Fig. 5a(ii) and Fig. 5b(ii)). The process mimics the depolarization and hyperpolarization behaviors observed in synaptic systems, offering a physically interpretable framework for neuromorphic signal modulation.

Figure 5c presents the conductance retention of the device under single Vp modulation at varying amplitudes. Owing to the migration potential barrier of Cl− ions, the device demonstrates robust retention exceeding 300 s. Nonlinear fitting of the conductance states under different Vp from −5 to −9 V reveals a distinct nonlinear correlation between Vp and conductance states, facilitating linear mapping between image pixels and Vp for effective background noise suppression (Supplementary Figs. 29 and 30). Furthermore, single Vp modulation with a nonlinear conductance response was applied for denoising preprocessing on an image of the word ‘HUST’, embedded with random background noise (σ=0.8). The processed image exhibited significantly enhanced contrast between the letters and background, with the effect sustained for over 300 s (Supplementary Fig. 31). To further explore conductance modulation, a pulse sequence of 100 negative Vp (−7 V) pulses and 100 positive Vp (5.5 V) pulses were applied, each with a duration and interval of 0.2 s (Fig. 5d). This sequence effectively emulated postsynaptic current (PSC) plasticity, exhibiting signal enhancement (depolarization) and suppression (hyperpolarization) characteristics. The observed PSC variations mimic key neurobiological behaviors, specifically pulse-number-dependent long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD). Figure 5e illustrates the current variation of the device over 45 cycles of 9000-pulse programming, demonstrating excellent robustness at fixed read voltages (−0.5 V, 0 V, and 0.5 V). Moreover, the device performance shows almost no degradation before and after 9000 pulse operations (Supplementary Fig. 32). These results highlight its potential for artificial synapse applications.

By leveraging the nonlinear conductance characteristics of Vp programming control (Supplementary Fig. 29) and the linear LTP/LTD behavior of Vp programming control (Fig. 5d), we developed an integrated preprocessing system coupled with a three-layer artificial neural network (ANN) to recognize the Fashion Modified National Institute of Standard and Technology (Fashion-MNIST) images (Fig. 5f). A detailed description of the system model is presented in Supplementary Fig. 33. To evaluate the device’s potential for background noise suppression, we introduced random background noise (σ=0.8) to the Fashion-MNIST images, with the preprocessed images (Supplementary Fig. 34a and 34b). The results demonstrate that preprocessing significantly facilitated convergence. After just 5 training epochs, the classification accuracy of preprocessed images reached 90.9%, notably surpassing the 80.7% achieved by unprocessed images (Fig. 5g). The corresponding confusion matrix for classification accuracy is depicted in Supplementary Fig. 35. By 20 epochs, the model attained an impressive classification accuracy of approximately 99.1%.

In summary, we present a single-crystalline ionic dielectric, Sb4O5Cl2, featuring oriented ion-migration channels and high ionic polarization, enabling a high dielectric constant of 23.3 (~25 nm) and precise carrier modulation. Through van der Waals integration with MoS2, the fabricated 2D FETs achieve good performance, including a high Ion/Ioff (109), low leakage current (10−14 A), and room-temperature mobility of 33.4 cm2 V−1 s−1 and realize various logic functions. The material further facilitates controllable and non-volatile transition between quasi-metallic and semiconducting state in MoS2, demonstrating 100-cycle reversibility, driven by electric-field-modulated Cl− ions accumulation and depletion at the Sb4O5Cl2/MoS2 interface, which shifts the Ef of MoS2. Based on this mechanism, memory functionality has been achieved with good retention (more than 3000 s), and endurance (over 1000 cycles). Leveraging these properties, we realized neuromorphic devices with synapse-like functions for integrated image storage, processing, and recognition, achieving 90.9% accuracy after 5 training epochs and sustaining non-volatile preprocessing for over 300 s. Our work provides an ionic dielectric material with precise carrier regulation capabilities for developing functional devices and manufacturing advanced electronics.
paper_content.methods:
Sample synthesis
Single crystals of bulk Sb4O5Cl2 were synthesized by the chemical vapor transport method. The mixture of Sb2O3 powder (Aladdin, 99.9%) and SbCl3 lump (Aladdin, 99.9%) in a molar ratio of 5:2 were placed into a sealed quartz tube under vacuum 10⁻2 Pa. The tube was slowly heated to 823 K on the source zone (T1), while the sink zone (T2) was kept at 723 K. After 7 days, the white plate-like crystals were obtained on the sink zone. For more reaction route details see Supplementary Fig. 1. The nanosheets were isolated from bulk crystals by mechanical exfoliation and transferred to a 300 nm SiO2/Si substrate.

Characterizations
As-grown Sb4O5Cl2 crystals were examined by XRD (D2 phase, Bruker), optical microscope (BX51, Olympus), atomic force microscopy (AFM, Dimension Icon, Bruker), HAADF-STEM and EDS (Tecnai G2 F30, FEI). Raman spectra were performed by a confocal Raman system (Alpha300R, WITec) equipped with a 532 nm laser source. PFM and KPFM measurements were carried out on AFM platform, and different Vionic were applied using a digital source meter (Keithley 2400).

Device fabrication and measurements
To achieve efficient exfoliation and targeted transfer, a two-step method was adopted (as shown in Supplementary Fig. 2). Firstly, scotch tape was used to mechanically exfoliate the Sb4O5Cl2 and transfer them onto the thermally releasable adhesive. Subsequently, the adhesive was heated to release the nanosheets onto a 300 nm SiO2/Si substrate. In this way, more and thinner Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheets could be obtained. Then, to enable targeted transfer, polypropylene carbonate (PPC) solution was first spin-coated and dried at 100 oC for 5 min. After that, polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) was used to simultaneously transfer the PPC/Sb4O5Cl2 onto the target 2D material (mechanically exfoliated FLG or MoS2).

The metal-insulator-metal capacitors were fabricated as follows: exfoliated FLG was used as bottom electrodes on 300 nm SiO2/Si. The Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheets were transferred onto the bottom electrode using the method described above. The top electrodes were deposited with In/Au (10/40 nm) after electron-beam lithography (EBL). For the back-gate MoS2/Sb4O5Cl2/FLG FETs, MoS2, Sb4O5Cl2, and FLG nanosheets were sequentially transferred and stacked on 300 nm SiO2/Si. Subsequently, after EBL, source-drain electrodes and back-gate electrodes were evaporated onto MoS2 and FLG. For the dual-gate Sb4O5Cl2/MoS2/SiO2 FETs, the fabrication method is the same as back-gate FETs. The electrical measurements were carried out with a semiconductor characterization system (4200SCS, Keithley) and a cryogenic probe station (CRX-6.5, Lake Shore).

Computational methods
We perform the first-principles calculations within the frame of the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) proposed by Perdew, Burke, and Ernzerhof (PBE)58 in the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP)59. The 5p, 5s were taken as valence states for Sb, 3s and 3p for Cl, and 2s, 2p for O atoms. The cutoff energy was chosen to 600 eV. The Γ centered k-grids were adopted 6×6×2. The convergence criterion of energy in relaxation was set to be 10⁻5 eV. We fully relaxed the atomic positions until the maximum force on each atom was less than 10⁻2 eV/Å. The Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (HSE06) hybrid functional60 was employed for the validation of band structures. The Brillouin zone path of the energy band is Γ-X-S-Y-Γ. In order to compute energy barriers, the CINEB method with 8 intermediate images was used to find the transition pathways61. The climbing image method allows for more accurate finding of saddle points with fewer images than the regular NEB method. To simulate the vertical Cl− migration path, a 2×1×1 supercell was constructed along a direction.

Implementation of pattern preprocessing and recognition
To integrate image preprocessing and classification, we employ the Fashion MNIST dataset with σ=0.8 random background noise and preprocess the images using a voltage-dependent nonlinear conductance function (Supplementary Fig. 30). In forward propagation, the preprocessed images are flattened and transformed via a nonlinear transformation using the ReLU activation function: h0 = max (0, x), yielding the hidden layer output h0. The hidden layer output is subsequently processed by a Softmax activation function to obtain the final probability distribution: Softmax(y0i) = Pey0i / Σj ey0j. reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript reports on the development of a single-crystalline ionic dielectric, featuring oriented Cl migration channels and a high dielectric constant. The material is integrated with MoS2 to fabricate 2D transistors exhibiting excellent performance metrics, including an on/off ratio exceeding 10**9, low leakage current and high mobility. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate a reversible, non-volatile metal-semiconductor transition in MoS2 through electric-field-controlled Cl⁻ ion migration. The work is technically solid and introduces a compelling dielectric platform for future 2D electronics. However, several critical aspects require clarification and strengthening before publication.
Major Points:
1) Stability and Variability Analysis is Insufficient: The title and claims of the manuscript suggest that Sb₄O₅Cl₂ is a viable dielectric for robust 2D electronics. However, the current work lacks comprehensive assessment of **device variability and long-term operational stability**. There is no data on device-to-device variation, bias stress reliability, or environmental stability, all of which are critical for practical applications. I recommend the authors include:
* Variability analysis across multiple devices (e.g., threshold voltage, on/off ratio, and mobility distribution).
* Endurance measurements beyond the reported 100 cycles (e.g., ≥10³ or 10⁴ phase switching cycles).
* BTI or TDDB data
* Retention stability under ambient and elevated temperature conditions (preferably >10³ s).
2) Ionic Migration and Retention Behavior: The authors describe a Cl⁻ ion migration barrier of ~2.1 eV, which is reasonable. However, more detailed quantification of retention behavior under real operating conditions is needed. The reported retention time of >300 s for conductance states and >1200 s for phase configuration is promising but should be extended and compared with standard non-volatile memory benchmarks. Additionally, any signs of ion migration-induced fatigue, spatial drift, or permanent degradation with repeated operation should be discussed.
3) Neuromorphic Demonstration Lacks Physical Validation: While the authors propose neuromorphic functionality through ion-mediated conductance modulation and simulate its application to image preprocessing and recognition (e.g., Fashion-MNIST dataset), this part remains entirely theoretical. The neuromorphic section relies solely on numerical simulations of an artificial neural network (ANN), with no hardware-level demonstration or integration of actual devices into a functional ANN system. Given the lack of experimental demonstration, this section currently lacks novelty and overstates the practical implications of the work. It is recommended that the neuromorphic content be either significantly condensed or removed unless supported by a physical implementation or hardware prototype. Alternatively, this section could be reframed to clearly emphasize its exploratory nature and potential future directions.
4) Absence of Circuit-Level Demonstrations: Although the device shows excellent performance metrics, the manuscript would benefit from including simple circuit demonstrations—such as a logic inverter, a memory cell, or an analog computing element—to better support the claim of “multifunctional two-dimensional electronics.” Presenting functional circuits would highlight the integration capability and practical utility of Sb₄O₅Cl₂ beyond the material level.
5) How stable is Sb₄O₅Cl₂ under prolonged gate bias? Are there any indications of performance drift or hysteresis with repeated cycles?
6) Have the authors observed any irreversible degradation or shift in threshold voltage across devices after multiple programming cycles?
7) Can the dielectric be integrated into scalable device platforms with channel lengths below 100 nm?
8) Can a basic logic or memory function be demonstrated to support claims of multifunctionality?
Minor Comments and Clarifications:
1) The term *“biomimetic”* used in the context of neuromorphic image processing is overstated. Since there is no biological interfacing or experimentally validated mimicry of neural functions, the term should be replaced with *“bio-inspired”* or qualified appropriately.
2) Please clarify whether the reported ultralow leakage current remains stable after repeated modulation cycles or environmental exposure.
3) The device architecture includes both top and bottom gates. A clearer explanation of their respective roles and independent control during modulation experiments would be helpful.
4) Can the dielectric thickness be scaled below 100 nm while maintaining the dielectric strength and performance?

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Exploring dielectrics with high gate capacitance and artificial tailoring of electronic states is highly desirable for the development of 2D electronics. Here, we report the synthesis of a single-crystalline ionic dielectric Sb4O5Cl2 with aligned ionic channels, achieving a dielectric constant of 23.3 (at a thickness of ~25 nm) and non-volatile programmable regulation of the ionic migration. The fabricated 2D MoS2 transistors display on/off ratios up to 109, leakage currents down to 10−14 A, and mobility of 33.4 cm2 V−1 s−1. Oriented ionic channels facilitate efficient and controllable migration of Cl− ions, thus realizing a non-structural-damage and reconfigurable transition between a quasi-metallic and semiconducting state in MoS2, with a retention time exceeding 3000 s. During 100 cycles of state transitions, the quasi-metallic state exhibits a conductivity of 10−5 S, which is 103 times that of the semiconducting state. Bio-inspired ionic channel further allows neuromorphic devices to integrate image storage, processing, and recognition capabilities, achieving a recognition accuracy improvement from 80.7% to 90.9% within just 5 training epochs through non-volatile preprocessing lasting over 300 s. Our study highlights the significant potential of this single-crystal ionic dielectric as a promising platform for fundamental research on electronic state modulation and advanced electronics.

---

## Introduction

Two-dimensional (2D) electronics have emerged as an ideal platform for studying exotic quantum physics, new functional transistors, and novel computing paradigms, owing to the quantum size effects, the tunable electronic structures, and the strong coupling interactions with external fields of 2D materials1–8. To meet the demands of increasingly complex functionalities, gate dielectrics need not only high dielectric constants to address device-scaling challenges9–12, but also artificial tailoring of electronic states13,14. This dual functionality may allow monolithic integration of multiple operational modes within a single device architecture, such as combining high-performance field-effect transistors (FETs) for digital logic operations15–17, reversible phase transition for analog memory programming18,19, and neuromorphic computing20,21 or other advanced functions. Yet now, conventional metal oxide dielectrics (such as Al2O3, SiO2, and HfO2) still face challenges including low dielectric constants, amorphous structures, and incompatible interfaces induced by dangling bonds, which hinders further miniaturization of devices, limited carrier modulation capabilities and lacking memory characteristics22–26.

In recent years, ionic gate dielectrics have attracted significant attention due to their high-κ dielectric constants from ionic polarization27–29 and the extremely high electric fields enabled by the electric double layer (EDL) of ions30–33, which can significantly enhance the capability of modulating electronic states in 2D materials inducing discrete superconducting phases34, strong Ising-type spin-orbit coupling33, and quenching the bandgap of 2D semiconductors32. However, conventional ionic dielectrics (liquid or solid electrolytes, primarily amorphous or polycrystalline structures) still present formidable challenges including poor compatibility with 2D materials, disordered ion migration pathways leading to random electrical performance and irreversible lattice damage caused by ion-migration resulting in poor stability, thereby severely limiting further research35–38.

In this work, we report a single-crystalline ionic dielectric Sb4O5Cl2, possessing a high κ exceeding 23.3 (~25 nm) and oriented ion-migration paths to address the above mentioned long-term issues. Benefiting from the high κ value and van der Waals structure, 2D transistors exhibit high on/off ratio (109) at a low operation voltage (Vds = 0.5 V), low leakage current (10−14 A), and high room-temperature mobility of 33.4 cm2 V−1 s−1, and realize NOT (inverter), AND, and NAND logic functions. The periodic ionic channels within the single-crystalline structure enhance the efficiency of ionic migration while achieving precise control and non-volatile characteristics. By electrically modulating the ionic states in Sb4O5Cl2, a reversible transition between quasi-metallic and semiconducting states in MoS2 channels has been achieved. This reconfigurability remains stable over 100 cycles and exhibits good retention under both room-temperature and elevated-temperature conditions (over 40 min). The quasi-metallic state shows a conductivity of ~10−5 S, surpassing the semiconducting state by three orders of magnitude, while the ion on/off ratios differ by six orders. Based on this, the device shows good memory properties with good retention (more than 3000 s) and endurance (over 1000 cycles). Furthermore, synapse-like functions integrating image storage, processing, and recognition have been realized. Owing to the non-volatile preprocessing capability lasting over 300 s, the recognition accuracy reaches 90.9% after just 5 training epochs. In summary, our research not only provides a material platform for high-performance 2D electronic devices but also demonstrates its potential in fields such as fundamental studies and multifunctional devices.

---

## Results

Characterization of Sb4O5Cl2 and theory calculations
The Sb4O5Cl2 single crystal, a type of ionic layered material crystallizing in the monoclinic system with space group P2/c (No. 14, a=6.16 Å, b=5.14 Å, c=13.62 Å), features an alternating stack of negatively charged [Cl]2n- anion layers and positively charged [Sb4O5]2n+ layers along the a-axis, exhibiting an interlayer spacing of approximately 6.16 Å (the left part of Fig. 1a). Notably, the Sb and O atoms in the [Sb4O5]2n+ layers are not densely packed. Instead, they form [SbO] eight-membered rings, which align precisely with the interlayer Cl− ions, thereby creating a pathway for Cl− ions migration along the a-axis between layers (the right part of Fig. 1a). Compared with amorphous and polycrystalline ionic materials, the oriented ion-migration within such a single-crystal system under external stimulus facilitates higher ionic concentration accumulation at interfaces, thereby inducing enhanced modulation and coupling effects. The synthesis method of Sb4O5Cl2 single crystals is provided in Methods and Supplementary Fig. 1. The as-synthesized centimeter-scale Sb4O5Cl2 single crystals exhibit three intense and sharp diffraction peaks assigned to the {100} crystallographic planes (Fig. 1b). Although the interlayers in Sb4O5Cl2 are bonded via weak electrostatic interactions-making it more difficult to exfoliate than traditional van der Waals 2D materials-nanosheets were still obtained using a thermally assisted tape exfoliation and transfer method (see Supplementary Fig. 2 and Methods). The obtained Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheets were further confirmed by Raman spectroscopy, and the vibrational modes of their characteristic peaks are assigned via angle-resolved polarized Raman measurements (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4). These characterizations indicate the highly crystalline layered structure of the as-synthesized Sb4O5Cl2 crystals.

To further elucidate the structure of Sb4O5Cl2, high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) characterization was conducted on Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheets. As shown in Fig. 1c, d and Supplementary Fig. 5, we performed HAADF-STEM imaging along different crystallographic orientations of Sb4O5Cl2, namely, [010], [100], and [001], all of which match well with the structure model and lattice spacing of Sb4O5Cl2. Given the contrast dependence of HAADF-STEM on the atomic number (Z) and atomic occupancy39–41, atomic columns containing different quantities of Sb (Z=51) are clearly identified. Notably, the unique interlayer Cl− ions sandwiched between [Sb4O5]2n+ layers can be distinctly observed (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 6) with an interlayer spacing of 6.16 Å. The measured lattice spacings of 6.81 Å and 5.14 Å correspond to the (002) and (010) lattice planes, respectively. While O atoms remain indiscernible due to their weak contrast arising from a low atomic number, Cl− ions confined within the [SbO] rings are clearly resolved with discernible intensity (Supplementary Fig. 7). Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping shows a uniform elemental distribution with an atomic ratio of Sb/O/Cl close to 4:5:2 (Supplementary Fig. 8). Furthermore, high-resolution EDS analysis along the [010] zone axis reveals an alternating stacked distribution of Sb and Cl elements (Fig. 1e), in agreement with the corresponding TEM image. Figure 1f displays the contrast intensity profile extracted along the orange dashed line crossing the [Sb4O5]2n+ layers and the pink dashed line situated within the interlayer regions from Fig. 1c. The profile distinctly reveals the periodic arrangement of Sb and Cl, along with the occupancy of Cl within the interlayer positions. The chemical states of Sb4O5Cl2 were further characterized by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), where the Cl 2p spectral feature centered at a binding energy of 197.7 eV provides conclusive evidence for the existence of interlayer Cl− ions (Supplementary Fig. 9).

We calculated the band structures of Sb4O5Cl2 using density functional theory (Fig. 1g). Sb4O5Cl2 exhibits a large indirect bandgap of ~3.7 eV, whose conduction band minimum (CBM) and valence band maximum (VBM) are located at Z and Γ point of the first Brillouin zone, respectively. Furthermore, the band structure of Sb4O5Cl2 was experimentally determined by ultraviolet-visible absorption spectrum and ultraviolet photoelectron spectrum (UPS) with a bandgap of ~3.9 eV (Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. 10), in good agreement with the calculated band structures. Such a wide bandgap renders Sb4O5Cl2 an insulator, as ascertained by the conductive test of a two-terminal device and its resistivity of over 1010 Ω·cm at 300 K can be extracted from the Ids-Vds curve (Supplementary Fig. 11).

Dielectric properties of Sb4O5Cl2
The theoretical dielectric constant of Sb4O5Cl2 was also calculated in Fig. 2a. Sb4O5Cl2 exhibits high dielectric constants across all three crystallographic directions, predominantly originating from ionic polarization (with electronic polarization contributing merely ~5 to the total permittivity). This observation highlights the strong ionic character of Sb4O5Cl2, which arises from its unique crystal structure. Notably, the highest dielectric constant of 32.9 is observed along the a-axis (perpendicular to the [Sb4O5]2n+ layers), which is consistent with the direction of the Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheets obtained by mechanical exfoliation, suggesting a high dielectric controllability of electronic states. The parallel-plate capacitors with vertical metal-insulator-metal (MIM) structure were further fabricated16, as shown in the inset of Fig. 2b. The effective dielectric constant (εeff) of Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheets can be calculated by the equation C = Aε0εeff/t, where C is the measured capacitance, A is the overlapping area of top and bottom electrodes, ε0 is the vacuum dielectric constant and t is the physical thickness of Sb4O5Cl2. The εeff of the 190 nm Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheet, derived from capacitance-frequency (C-f) measurement (Fig. 2b), reaches around 29.5 at 100 kHz and this experimental value aligns remarkably well with theoretical calculations. Thickness-dependent εeff is shown in Fig. 2c. Despite thickness-dependent reduction, Sb4O5Cl2 achieves a dielectric constant of up to 43.2 and maintains a value above 17.5 even at ~15 nm, attributable to its strong ionic polarization mechanism. Additionally, the leakage current and corresponding breakdown field strength of Sb4O5Cl2 were demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 12, revealing a breakdown field of 3 MV cm−1 while maintaining leakage current below the dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) limit9. The relationship between the bandgap and corresponding dielectric constant of currently reported dielectrics was plotted in Fig. 2d9–11,17,28,29,39,42–47, demonstrating that Sb4O5Cl2 single crystal possesses a relatively higher dielectric constant (as evidenced by εeff = 3.3 for h-BN, εeff = 16.5 for β-Bi2SeO5, εeff = 11.5 for Sb2O3, εeff = 8.4 for CaF2 and εeff = 15.3 for GdOCl).

Single-crystalline ionic dielectric Sb4O5Cl2 for 2D transistors
To examine the potential of Sb4O5Cl2 as a dielectric in devices, MoS2 FETs with Sb4O5Cl2 as the bottom-gate dielectric were fabricated on the SiO2/Si substrate, utilizing exfoliated few-layer graphene (FLG) as gate electrode and In/Au as the source and drain electrodes. Figure 2e shows linear Ids-Vds curves under different gate voltages (Vg), indicating well electrical contacts. The transfer characteristics are presented in Fig. 2f, presenting a high on/off ratio (Ion/Ioff) exceeding 109 at a low operation voltage (Vds = 0.5 V). It is worth noting that even when the operation voltage of Vds is as low as 0.05 V, the transistor still maintains a high Ion/Ioff of 108. Moreover, the device exhibits a low leakage current (~10−14 A) throughout the entire testing process. Furthermore, field-effect mobility of the device reaches 33.4 cm2 V−1 s−1 by linear fitting the transfer curve (Vds = 1 V). The high Ion/Ioff and charge carrier mobility are fundamentally attributed to the superior dielectric constant of Sb4O5Cl2, which originates from robust ionic polarization effects enabled by its ordered ionic migration channels. And the performance of 20 FETs devices was tested and statistically analyzed, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 13. The results demonstrate that the devices exhibit relatively excellent performance in terms of Ion/Ioff, threshold voltage, and mobility, with relatively small variations observed between different devices. Additionally, we fabricated and characterized a top-gated MoS2 device with a Sb4O5Cl2 single-crystal dielectric layer thinner than 100 nm (Supplementary Fig. 14), which also exhibits a high Ion/Ioff exceeding 108. Compared with the 2D transistors with state-of-the-art high-κ dielectrics, our devices exhibit stronger gate controllability (as shown in Fig. 2g), exhibiting higher Ion/Ioff under low operation voltage and much lower leakage current9–11,17,28,29,39,43,44. To evaluate the stability of the Sb4O5Cl2 ionic single-crystal dielectric layer, we conducted positive bias temperature instability (PBTI) and time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) tests on the MoS2/Sb4O5Cl2/FLG device, and the results are presented in Supplementary Fig. 15.

We also fabricated logic circuits based on MoS2/Sb4O5Cl2 and MoTe2/Sb4O5Cl2 FETs. Supplementary Fig. 16 illustrates the most essential NOT gate (also known as an inverter), which exhibits sharp switching characteristics at different VDD values. More complicated logic units such as the AND gate and the NAND gate were also fabricated (Supplementary Fig. 17). The AND gate and NAND gate operate at VDD of 2.0 V to perform their logical functions. Our results confirm the application potential of the Sb4O5Cl2 ionic single-crystal dielectric layer in logic circuits.

Reconfigurable transition of MoS2
The ion-electron coupling between Sb4O5Cl2 and MoS2 can effectively modulate the carrier concentration in MoS2, thereby further inducing changes in the electrical properties of MoS2. As illustrated in Fig. 3a, the top Sb4O5Cl2 layer functions as a modulation layer, not merely a dielectric. It regulates the direction of Cl− ion migration within itself by adjusting the top ionic gate voltage (Vionic), thus controlling the carrier concentration in MoS2. The SiO2/Si back-gate, in contrast, is used to characterize the modulated electrical behavior of the MoS2 channel.

The Ids-Vds and back-gate transfer characteristics under varying Vionic (+10 V and −10 V for 20 s) are characterized, with the results presented in Fig. 3b, c, respectively. From the Ids-Vds curves, it can be observed that, compared to pristine MoS2, a positive Vionic suppresses Ids while a negative Vionic enhances Ids, which indicates that applying Vionic can effectively modulate the conductivity of MoS2. From the back-gate transfer characteristics, a positive Vionic enhances the n-type semiconductor behavior of MoS2, increasing the Ion/Ioff from 106 to 107. In contrast, after applying a negative Vionic, the device maintains a high conductance state (Ids ~ 10−5 A) throughout the back-gate sweep process, and the Ion/Ioff is less than 10, indicating the transition from semiconducting to quasi-metallic characteristics. Importantly, unlike structure-destructive and irreversible atomic doping48,49, the transition of MoS2 between quasi-metallic and semiconducting state enabled by the modulated Cl− ions of Sb4O5Cl2 exhibits non-destructive nature and high reversibility. By applying gradually increasing negative and positive Vionic to the Sb4O5Cl2 modulation layer, a stepwise transition of MoS2 between semiconducting and quasi-metallic state was achieved, as shown in Fig. 3d, e, respectively. We also tested the retention characteristics of both states at room temperature and elevated temperatures (Supplementary Fig. 18). The state could be maintained for over 40 min even at 100 °C. Furthermore, (Ids-T) curves after different pulsed Vionic demonstrate that the conductance retention can exceed 3000 s (Supplementary Fig. 19). These results indicate that the reconfigurable modulation exhibits a certain degree of non-volatility, and based on this, we successfully fabricated a memory device with good retention (>3000 s) and endurance (>1000 cycles), as shown in Supplementary Fig. 20.

Notably, this reconfigurable transition exhibits good cycling stability. As shown in Fig. 3f, the device underwent 100 cycles of positive-negative Vionic switching while maintaining stable state transfer characteristics. With increasing cycling times, both the quasi-metallic and semiconducting state exhibit minimal fluctuations in Ion/Ioff (Fig. 3g). After 100 cycles, the quasi-metallic state retains an Ion/Ioff below 10, while the semiconducting state maintains a high Ion/Ioff of 105. As demonstrated in Fig. 3h, the quasi-metallic state consistently maintains high conductance (>10−5 S), which is 103 times higher than that of the semiconducting state, while a seven-order-of-magnitude conductance contrast between the two states persists even after 100 cycling tests (Vbg = −10 V). Furthermore, the reconfiguration endurance was extended to 2000 cycles with stable performance. The performance of Sb4O5Cl2-based top-gate FETs was compared before and after cycling, and negligible degradation was observed (Supplementary Fig. 21). These results demonstrate that Sb4O5Cl2 exhibits a remarkably strong non-volatile modulation capability on the electronic states of MoS2, and owing to its unique crystal structure, the physical structural damage caused by this modulation is negligible50.

Mechanism of oriented ion-migration in Sb4O5Cl2
To elucidate the mechanism of tailoring the electronic states, theoretical calculations and systematic experiments were conducted. Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) measurements on Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheets ruled out ferroelectric behavior, supported by negligible phase hysteresis and butterfly amplitude loops40, consistent with its centrosymmetric structure (Supplementary Fig. 22). Therefore, we proposed that the migration of Cl− ions at the Sb4O5Cl2/MoS2 interface under the top ionic gate leads to the tailoring of electronic states in MoS2, enabling reconfigurable transitions between quasi-metallic and semiconducting state, as illustrated in Fig. 4a. Under negative Vionic, Cl− ions migrate and accumulate at the Sb4O5Cl2/MoS2 interface, which captures holes in the MoS2 channel, thereby generating more electrons and driving the transition of MoS2 from the initial n-type semiconductor to a quasi-metal. While under positive Vionic, Cl− ions at the interface are depleted, leading to the accumulation of Cl− vacancies (VCl). These VCl capture electrons in the MoS2 channel, reducing the electron concentration and restoring semiconducting behavior. Subsequently, we conducted band structure calculations for MoS2 at two distinct Sb4O5Cl2 interfaces-the Cl− ions interface and the VCl interface-as well as for isolated MoS2, as shown in Fig. 4b, c and Supplementary Fig. 23, respectively. The Fermi level (Ef) of isolated MoS2 is located at the VBM. However, MoS2 shows an upward Ef shift into the conduction band with Cl− ion interface, indicating n-type degenerate doping48. In contrast, the Ef of MoS2 returns to the VBM position with Cl− vacancy interfaces closely matching that of the isolated MoS2, indicating that MoS2 exhibits semiconducting properties at this state. The theoretical calculation results are in excellent agreement with the experimental data and the proposed mechanism.

Furthermore, the ion-migration paths have been calculated, as shown in Fig. 4d. The total energy of the system at each step as the Cl− ions moved through the [Sb4O5]2n+ layer was obtained by relaxing the atomic positions until the maximum force on each atom was less than 10⁻2 eV/Å. To enable efficient Cl− ions migration, the Sb-O bonds surrounding the [SbO] octagonal ring undergo sequential dissociation, driving structural reconfiguration from an octagonal ring through decagonal to dodecagonal configurations, with the entire process exhibiting an energy barrier of 2.10 eV. Compared to ion-migration barriers in other 2D material systems (Fig. 4e)51–53, the Cl− ions migration barrier in Sb4O5Cl2 single crystals is relatively lower (e.g., K+/MoS2: 2.46 eV and Ag+/graphene: 4.27 eV) indicating the inherent migration. Meanwhile, the periodic lattice potential of the single-crystalline Sb4O5Cl2 constrains Cl− migration, imparting a certain degree of non-volatility.

To further confirm this modulation mechanism, we fabricated a MoS2/Sb4O5Cl2/FLG device and employed Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) to characterize the surface potential evolution (Supplementary Fig. 24). As shown in Fig. 4f and Supplementary Fig. 25, the change in the work function is expressed by the contact potential difference (CPD) between the sample surface and the probe tip, as defined by the formula VCPD = (φtip − φsample)/q, where q is the elementary charge, φsample and φtip are the work functions of the sample surface and probe tip54,55. Compared with the pristine KPFM mapping, at Vionic = −20 V, the potential of Sb4O5Cl2 in the edge regions of MoS2 exhibits a significant decrease, which correlates with an increase in the φsample and a downwards shift of the Ef, attributed to the reduction in electron concentration resulting from the accumulation of Cl− ions. Conversely, at Vionic = +20 V, the potential of Sb4O5Cl2 at the MoS2 edges exhibits a significant increase, accompanied by an upward shift of the Ef, as Cl− ions migrate away from the interface, resulting in hole depletion and electron accumulation. Notably, the potential variation in Sb4O5Cl2 was exclusively observed within the overlap regions between the bottom FLG and the top MoS2 layer. This phenomenon is attributed to the migration of Cl− ions occurring only in areas subjected to a vertical electric field, whereas ions migration remains negligible in non-gated regions (as demarcated by the black dashed lines in Fig. 4f). The potential-distance profiles extracted along the yellow and red arrows (Fig. 4f) are shown in Fig. 4g and Supplementary Fig. 26. Initially, the regulated (left part of the black dashed line) and non-regulated (right part of the black dashed line) MoS2 regions exhibited a minor potential difference (−18.2 mV). At Vionic = −20 V, the regulated MoS2 region showed an Ef upshift and potential increase, resulting in a 110.6 mV difference compared to the non-regulated region. Conversely, at Vionic = +20 V, the potential difference reversed to −84.3 mV, indicating an Ef downshift in the regulated MoS2 region that exceeded its initial state (Fig. 4g). The Sb4O5Cl2 at MoS2 edges displayed significant potential inversion (>2 V, Supplementary Fig. 26) under alternating Vionic, driven by Cl− ions depletion and accumulation. KPFM results reveal the band structure evolution of the Sb4O5Cl2/MoS2 heterojunction under varying Vionic (Supplementary Fig. 27), with the Ef shift in MoS2 in excellent agreement with electrical and theoretical data. This highlight that the reconfigurable transition between quasi-metallic and semiconducting state in MoS2 is achieved through efficient Cl− ions migration enabled by the unique crystal structure of Sb4O5Cl2.

Neuromorphic image preprocessing and classification
Leveraging the distinct periodic crystal potential field and the tunable Cl− ions migration behavior of Sb4O5Cl2, we emulate ion-mediated conductance modulation analogous to synaptic plasticity. The detailed biological analogy and transport mechanism are provided in Supplementary Information (Supplementary Fig. 28)56,57. Under positive or negative pulse voltages (Vp), Cl− ions drift directionally within the dielectric, accumulating near or depleting from the MoS2 interface through [SbO] ring channels, as illustrated in Fig. 5a(i), b(i). This dynamic redistribution modulates the local Cl− concentration, thereby tuning the device conductance (Fig. 5a(ii) and Fig. 5b(ii)). The process mimics the depolarization and hyperpolarization behaviors observed in synaptic systems, offering a physically interpretable framework for neuromorphic signal modulation.

Figure 5c presents the conductance retention of the device under single Vp modulation at varying amplitudes. Owing to the migration potential barrier of Cl− ions, the device demonstrates robust retention exceeding 300 s. Nonlinear fitting of the conductance states under different Vp from −5 to −9 V reveals a distinct nonlinear correlation between Vp and conductance states, facilitating linear mapping between image pixels and Vp for effective background noise suppression (Supplementary Figs. 29 and 30). Furthermore, single Vp modulation with a nonlinear conductance response was applied for denoising preprocessing on an image of the word ‘HUST’, embedded with random background noise (σ=0.8). The processed image exhibited significantly enhanced contrast between the letters and background, with the effect sustained for over 300 s (Supplementary Fig. 31). To further explore conductance modulation, a pulse sequence of 100 negative Vp (−7 V) pulses and 100 positive Vp (5.5 V) pulses were applied, each with a duration and interval of 0.2 s (Fig. 5d). This sequence effectively emulated postsynaptic current (PSC) plasticity, exhibiting signal enhancement (depolarization) and suppression (hyperpolarization) characteristics. The observed PSC variations mimic key neurobiological behaviors, specifically pulse-number-dependent long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD). Figure 5e illustrates the current variation of the device over 45 cycles of 9000-pulse programming, demonstrating excellent robustness at fixed read voltages (−0.5 V, 0 V, and 0.5 V). Moreover, the device performance shows almost no degradation before and after 9000 pulse operations (Supplementary Fig. 32). These results highlight its potential for artificial synapse applications.

By leveraging the nonlinear conductance characteristics of Vp programming control (Supplementary Fig. 29) and the linear LTP/LTD behavior of Vp programming control (Fig. 5d), we developed an integrated preprocessing system coupled with a three-layer artificial neural network (ANN) to recognize the Fashion Modified National Institute of Standard and Technology (Fashion-MNIST) images (Fig. 5f). A detailed description of the system model is presented in Supplementary Fig. 33. To evaluate the device’s potential for background noise suppression, we introduced random background noise (σ=0.8) to the Fashion-MNIST images, with the preprocessed images (Supplementary Fig. 34a and 34b). The results demonstrate that preprocessing significantly facilitated convergence. After just 5 training epochs, the classification accuracy of preprocessed images reached 90.9%, notably surpassing the 80.7% achieved by unprocessed images (Fig. 5g). The corresponding confusion matrix for classification accuracy is depicted in Supplementary Fig. 35. By 20 epochs, the model attained an impressive classification accuracy of approximately 99.1%.

In summary, we present a single-crystalline ionic dielectric, Sb4O5Cl2, featuring oriented ion-migration channels and high ionic polarization, enabling a high dielectric constant of 23.3 (~25 nm) and precise carrier modulation. Through van der Waals integration with MoS2, the fabricated 2D FETs achieve good performance, including a high Ion/Ioff (109), low leakage current (10−14 A), and room-temperature mobility of 33.4 cm2 V−1 s−1 and realize various logic functions. The material further facilitates controllable and non-volatile transition between quasi-metallic and semiconducting state in MoS2, demonstrating 100-cycle reversibility, driven by electric-field-modulated Cl− ions accumulation and depletion at the Sb4O5Cl2/MoS2 interface, which shifts the Ef of MoS2. Based on this mechanism, memory functionality has been achieved with good retention (more than 3000 s), and endurance (over 1000 cycles). Leveraging these properties, we realized neuromorphic devices with synapse-like functions for integrated image storage, processing, and recognition, achieving 90.9% accuracy after 5 training epochs and sustaining non-volatile preprocessing for over 300 s. Our work provides an ionic dielectric material with precise carrier regulation capabilities for developing functional devices and manufacturing advanced electronics.

---

## Methods

Sample synthesis
Single crystals of bulk Sb4O5Cl2 were synthesized by the chemical vapor transport method. The mixture of Sb2O3 powder (Aladdin, 99.9%) and SbCl3 lump (Aladdin, 99.9%) in a molar ratio of 5:2 were placed into a sealed quartz tube under vacuum 10⁻2 Pa. The tube was slowly heated to 823 K on the source zone (T1), while the sink zone (T2) was kept at 723 K. After 7 days, the white plate-like crystals were obtained on the sink zone. For more reaction route details see Supplementary Fig. 1. The nanosheets were isolated from bulk crystals by mechanical exfoliation and transferred to a 300 nm SiO2/Si substrate.

Characterizations
As-grown Sb4O5Cl2 crystals were examined by XRD (D2 phase, Bruker), optical microscope (BX51, Olympus), atomic force microscopy (AFM, Dimension Icon, Bruker), HAADF-STEM and EDS (Tecnai G2 F30, FEI). Raman spectra were performed by a confocal Raman system (Alpha300R, WITec) equipped with a 532 nm laser source. PFM and KPFM measurements were carried out on AFM platform, and different Vionic were applied using a digital source meter (Keithley 2400).

Device fabrication and measurements
To achieve efficient exfoliation and targeted transfer, a two-step method was adopted (as shown in Supplementary Fig. 2). Firstly, scotch tape was used to mechanically exfoliate the Sb4O5Cl2 and transfer them onto the thermally releasable adhesive. Subsequently, the adhesive was heated to release the nanosheets onto a 300 nm SiO2/Si substrate. In this way, more and thinner Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheets could be obtained. Then, to enable targeted transfer, polypropylene carbonate (PPC) solution was first spin-coated and dried at 100 oC for 5 min. After that, polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) was used to simultaneously transfer the PPC/Sb4O5Cl2 onto the target 2D material (mechanically exfoliated FLG or MoS2).

The metal-insulator-metal capacitors were fabricated as follows: exfoliated FLG was used as bottom electrodes on 300 nm SiO2/Si. The Sb4O5Cl2 nanosheets were transferred onto the bottom electrode using the method described above. The top electrodes were deposited with In/Au (10/40 nm) after electron-beam lithography (EBL). For the back-gate MoS2/Sb4O5Cl2/FLG FETs, MoS2, Sb4O5Cl2, and FLG nanosheets were sequentially transferred and stacked on 300 nm SiO2/Si. Subsequently, after EBL, source-drain electrodes and back-gate electrodes were evaporated onto MoS2 and FLG. For the dual-gate Sb4O5Cl2/MoS2/SiO2 FETs, the fabrication method is the same as back-gate FETs. The electrical measurements were carried out with a semiconductor characterization system (4200SCS, Keithley) and a cryogenic probe station (CRX-6.5, Lake Shore).

Computational methods
We perform the first-principles calculations within the frame of the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) proposed by Perdew, Burke, and Ernzerhof (PBE)58 in the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP)59. The 5p, 5s were taken as valence states for Sb, 3s and 3p for Cl, and 2s, 2p for O atoms. The cutoff energy was chosen to 600 eV. The Γ centered k-grids were adopted 6×6×2. The convergence criterion of energy in relaxation was set to be 10⁻5 eV. We fully relaxed the atomic positions until the maximum force on each atom was less than 10⁻2 eV/Å. The Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (HSE06) hybrid functional60 was employed for the validation of band structures. The Brillouin zone path of the energy band is Γ-X-S-Y-Γ. In order to compute energy barriers, the CINEB method with 8 intermediate images was used to find the transition pathways61. The climbing image method allows for more accurate finding of saddle points with fewer images than the regular NEB method. To simulate the vertical Cl− migration path, a 2×1×1 supercell was constructed along a direction.

Implementation of pattern preprocessing and recognition
To integrate image preprocessing and classification, we employ the Fashion MNIST dataset with σ=0.8 random background noise and preprocess the images using a voltage-dependent nonlinear conductance function (Supplementary Fig. 30). In forward propagation, the preprocessed images are flattened and transformed via a nonlinear transformation using the ReLU activation function: h0 = max (0, x), yielding the hidden layer output h0. The hidden layer output is subsequently processed by a Softmax activation function to obtain the final probability distribution: Softmax(y0i) = Pey0i / Σj ey0j. The classification error is measured using the cross-entropy loss function: L = − Σi=1C yi log(pi), where C=10 denotes the total number of classes, yi is the true label in one-hot encoding, and pi is the predicted probability. In backpropagation, the Adam optimizer updates model parameters, following W = W − η ∂L/∂W, where η = 0.001 is the learning rate, and ∂L/∂W denotes the gradient of the loss function with respect to the weights. Notably, all network weights are mapped to conductance values based on the LTP/LTD characteristics (Supplementary Fig. 33, blue dashed box), ensuring adherence to the physical properties of the device.

This manuscript reports on the development of a single-crystalline ionic dielectric, featuring oriented Cl migration channels and a high dielectric constant. * Variability analysis across multiple devices (e.g., threshold voltage, on/off ratio, and mobility distribution).
* Endurance measurements beyond the reported 100 cycles (e.g., ≥10³ or 10⁴ phase switching cycles).
* BTI or TDDB data
* Retention stability under ambient and elevated temperature conditions (preferably >10³ s).
